marble.name: Physical vs Chemical Changes
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Distinguish between physical changes (reversible, no new substances formed) and chemical changes (new substances formed, often irreversible), using conservation of mass to understand both types
marble.prompt: If you dissolved sugar in tea versus burnt toast in the toaster, could they explain which is a physical change and which is a chemical change — and what test would show that mass is conserved in both cases?

cluster.summary: Your child is exploring the materials around them — identifying different substances like wood, plastic, and metal, and discovering their properties such as whether they're hard or soft, rough or smooth.

misconceptions: A change is chemical whenever the appearance changes (colour, state).
Mass changes during a chemical reaction (atoms created or destroyed).
Dissolving is a chemical change because the solid 'disappears'.
Physical changes are always easily reversible and chemical ones never.
New atoms are created in a reaction, rather than existing atoms being regrouped.
representations: A macro event synced to a particle window (molecules intact vs atoms regrouping)
A conserved-mass balance readout across the change
authoredAnswer: Physical: melting ice and dissolving sugar (no new substance — same stuff rearranged, reversible). Chemical: rusting (a NEW substance, iron oxide, forms). The rule: a CHEMICAL change makes one or more NEW substances (signalled by colour change, gas, temperature change, or a precipitate); a physical change makes none. Full marks rest the rule on 'new substance made?', not on 'is it reversible?'.
probe: Predict-Observe-Explain: add a spatula of copper sulfate to warm water (dissolves — physical) and, separately, drop an iron nail into copper sulfate solution (displacement — chemical, nail goes copper-coloured, blue fades). wrongAnswers.wrong: Rusting is chemical only because you can't undo it, and the others are physical because you can.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: classifies solely by whether it can be reversed; stumbles on reversible chemical changes or hard-to-reverse physical ones
wrongAnswers.fix: Shift the criterion to 'new substance made?'. Reversibility often correlates but isn't the definition — show a reversible chemical change and an awkward-to-reverse physical one.

wrongAnswers.wrong: Dissolving is chemical, because the sugar turns into a new substance in the tea.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: puts dissolving in the chemical pile, treating the solution as a new substance
wrongAnswers.fix: Dissolving makes a mixture, recoverable by evaporation; the sugar is unchanged. No new substance → physical. Reconnect to conservation and recovery.

wrongAnswers.wrong: Melting is chemical, because a solid turning into a liquid is a new substance.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: labels melting/boiling chemical because the appearance/state changed
wrongAnswers.fix: State changes rearrange the SAME particles — still water, no new substance. Use the particle picture to show identity is preserved.
